answer: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon. The electronegativity difference causes the halogen to pull electron density away from carbon, giving carbon a partial positive charge ($\delta+$) and the halogen a partial negative charge ($\delta-$). This electron-deficient carbon is susceptible to attack by nucleophiles.

answer: Bond polarity alone predicts: $$\mathrm{R\text{-}F > R\text{-}Cl > R\text{-}Br > R\text{-}I}$$ because C-F is the most polar bond (largest electronegativity difference), making carbon most electrophilic. However, the observed order is the reverse because **bond energy dominates**: the very strong C-F bond cannot be broken easily despite high polarity.

answer: Atomic size of the halogen increases down Group 17 (F → Cl → Br → I). A larger halogen atom forms a longer C-X bond with carbon, and longer bonds are weaker. Therefore bond energy decreases: C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I.

answer: $$\mathrm{R\text{-}I > R\text{-}Br > R\text{-}Cl > R\text{-}F}$$ Iodoalkanes are most reactive and fluoroalkanes are least reactive (essentially unreactive under ordinary conditions) because bond energy, not polarity, is the decisive factor.

answer: The two factors are **bond polarity** and **bond energy** of the C-X bond. **Bond energy is the dominant factor**: although the C-F bond is the most polar, the C-I bond is the weakest and easiest to break, making iodoalkanes the most reactive.
